opus-5.5.text:
I think the premise itself is worth pushing on a little, because "solving every mathematical problem" is not quite how mathematics works. There's no fixed list of problems sitting somewhere waiting to be checked off. A huge part of what mathematicians do is decide which questions are worth asking in the first place: which definitions are natural, which structures are interesting, which conjecture, if true, would reorganize how we understand a whole field. That's a matter of taste and judgment as much as technique.

So even in a world where AI is extraordinarily good at proving things, and I do believe we're heading toward systems that can prove very hard theorems, and do it in a formally verified way, the role of the mathematician shifts rather than disappears. I'd compare it to what happened when computers took over numerical computation. Nobody mourns that we no longer compute logarithm tables by hand. That freed people to think at a higher level.

I see a few roles. First, mathematicians become something like architects or directors. They set the research agenda, they decide what's meaningful, and they guide these systems toward questions that matter, whether for pure understanding or for physics, biology, or engineering.

Second, there's understanding. A proof that's correct but that no human can absorb is valuable, but it's not the end of the story. Mathematics is fundamentally a human activity of making sense of things. Someone has to take what the machine found and distill it: why is this true, what's the key idea, how does it connect to other things we know. That kind of explanation and synthesis becomes even more important.

Third, I think AI will actually bring many more people into mathematics. If verification is cheap and reliable, because a proof is checked formally in something like Lean, then a curious student or an engineer can explore ideas with a collaborator that never gets tired and never lets an error slip through. The barrier to doing real mathematics drops a lot.

And honestly, from my own experience, the joy of math was never only about getting the answer. It's the feeling of something clicking into place. AI doesn't take that away from anyone. People still play chess even though engines are far stronger, and chess is arguably more popular now than ever. I'm optimistic that mathematics will be similar: more people doing it, at a deeper level, with much more ambitious questions on the table.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians will distill AI-found proofs and explain why they are true and how they connect to known ideas.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing worthwhile questions and explaining proofs, but does not say that understanding AI-generated proofs leads mathematicians to formulate new conjectures.

r003.rationale: It says AI could support more ambitious mathematics, but does not state that AI’s discoveries enable mathematicians to invent better.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and honestly, I don't accept the premise that mathematicians disappear. I'd push back on it from a few directions.

First, "solving every problem" assumes the problems already exist. In mathematics, choosing the question is half the work, maybe more than half. Nobody handed Grothendieck a list of theorems to prove. He invented the language of schemes because he had a sense that certain things ought to be connected, long before he could state them precisely. That taste for which questions matter, which abstractions will be fertile, which conjectures are worth a decade of someone's life, is not something you get from a proof engine. Even if AI could prove any well-posed statement, someone still has to decide what's worth posing.

Second, a proof is not the same thing as understanding. If a system gives me a ten-thousand-line formal proof of the Riemann hypothesis, I'd be thrilled, but the community wouldn't be done. We'd want to know why it's true. We'd want the three-page version, the conceptual reason, the generalization. A lot of the history of mathematics is re-proving known results more beautifully. Mathematicians are, in a sense, the people who turn truth into insight, and I think that role gets more important, not less, when the supply of truths goes up.

Third, there's a practical thing I see every day working on this. The best mathematicians right now are becoming something like directors. They're setting the direction, verifying, spotting where the model is confidently wrong, and steering the search. The skill set shifts toward judgment and taste rather than grinding through calculations. That's a very different job from what a graduate student did in 1990, but I'd argue it's closer to what the great mathematicians always did.

And last, I think we'd be surprised how quickly the frontier moves. Every time a tool has made some class of problems trivial, whether it's Gaussian elimination, computer algebra, or SAT solvers, mathematicians didn't run out of things to do. They just started asking harder questions. I don't think mathematics is a finite pile of problems that can be exhausted. It's more like a space that keeps opening as you explore it.

So if AI becomes that capable, the role of a mathematician becomes: asking the right questions, interpreting the answers, and deciding what it all means. Which is, I'd say, the part that was always the most human anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians would seek the conceptual reason behind AI-generated proofs and turn proved truths into insight.

r002.rationale: It says mathematicians can pose worthwhile questions and generalize results, but does not state that understanding AI-generated proofs leads them to formulate new conjectures.

r003.rationale: It says AI-enabled results may prompt harder questions, but does not clearly propose that AI's mathematical discoveries enable mathematicians to invent better.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematicians would still have a role in deciding what’s worth asking. Solving a problem is one part of mathematics, but another part is creating definitions, noticing connections, and developing a perspective that makes things clearer.

Even if an AI could solve every problem we gave it, we might still want to understand why a result is true and how it fits into a larger picture. A proof can establish something without giving us that sense of understanding.

So I imagine the role would shift toward choosing questions and making meaning out of the answers. And mathematics would still be something people do for the joy of discovery, even if we weren’t the fastest at it.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians would still seek to understand why AI-solved results are true, and that a proof can establish a result without providing understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not say that understanding AI-generated proofs would lead mathematicians to formulate new conjectures.

r003.rationale: It discusses choosing questions and making meaning from answers, but does not say AI discoveries may enable mathematicians to invent better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematicians do more than solve problems. We decide which questions are worth asking, connect ideas that initially seem unrelated, and try to understand why something is true. Even if an AI could give us a proof of any statement, there would still be a difference between having that proof and understanding what it tells us.

So I imagine the role shifting toward choosing directions and making sense of the results. What new definitions should we introduce? Which answers reveal a broader principle? How does a mathematical idea change the way we think about another field?

And there's still something valuable about doing mathematics yourself. Knowing that a machine can solve a problem doesn't necessarily take away the joy of exploring it. But if AI could also ask the most interesting questions and explain every answer beautifully, then I think we'd have to be honest that the profession could change very radically. I wouldn't assume our current role is guaranteed to remain the same.
